hook.text: Design a URL shortener. Prompts like this one are where interviews have grown: fewer take-home projects, and more live design discussion, where every choice gets asked why.

plan.text: Five questions, and one design carried through all of them: how to start, what to estimate, the first diagram, what can take it down, and what goes in front of it.

q1.text: Question one. How do you approach an open-ended system design question? Not by drawing boxes. First, clarify the requirements, in two lists.

q1-func.text: Functional: what the system must do. Shorten a long URL, and send anyone who opens the short one to the long one. Then ask about the edges: custom aliases? Links that expire?

q1-nonfunc.text: Non-functional: scale, latency, availability and consistency. Redirects must be fast and almost never fail, and a short link must never start pointing somewhere else.

q1-steps.text: Then estimate the load, define the API, sketch a high-level design, and only then drill into the bottlenecks.

q1-why.text: The second list is the one that shapes the design: the same two features, at a thousand users or at a billion redirects a day, are different systems. Say each assumption out loud, so the interviewer can correct it before you build on it.

q2.text: Question two. What back-of-the-envelope numbers should you estimate? The ones that turn product scale into load: requests per second, or QPS, then storage and bandwidth.

q2-trick.text: One trick does most of the work. A million requests a day is about twelve a second.

q2-writes.text: So assume ten million new links a day: about a hundred and twenty writes a second.

q2-reads.text: Reads matter more. Most consumer systems are read-heavy, a hundred to one or more, so assume a hundred redirects per link: a billion a day, about twelve thousand a second.

q2-peak.text: Size for the peak, not the average. Peaks often run two to three times higher, so take three: about thirty-five thousand redirects a second.

q2-storage.text: Storage: a few hundred bytes a link, say five hundred, is five gigabytes a day, about nine terabytes in five years.

q2-band.text: Bandwidth: say half a kilobyte per redirect, and that peak is about seventeen megabytes a second.

q2-verdict.text: Neither is hard. This system is decided by its read traffic, and by how much of it a cache can answer.

q2-ladder.text: Then keep one picture in your head: what each level of memory and network costs. Main memory, a hundred nanoseconds. An SSD read, a thousand times that. A round trip inside the data center, five times more again. So count the network hops in a request before anything else.

q2-tail.text: And quote latency as a percentile, never a mean. In a simulated sample of forty thousand requests, the median takes twenty-four milliseconds and the mean thirty-one, but one request in a hundred takes two hundred and eighty-six or more: the ninety-ninth percentile.

q2-fanout.text: A page that makes a hundred calls, each with that one-in-a-hundred chance, hits at least one on sixty-three percent of loads.

q3.text: Question three. Design a URL shortener at a high level. Start from the API: one call takes a long URL and returns a short key, and the other takes the key and redirects.

q3-key.text: The key is base sixty-two: lowercase, uppercase and digits. Encode an auto-incrementing ID, and six characters hold fifty-seven billion links, over fifteen years at ten million a day.

q3-hash.text: Or hash the long URL and keep a few characters. If that key is taken, add a salt and hash again, and make the write conditional, so two servers can't both claim it.

q3-diagram.text: Store the mapping in a key-value store, since every lookup is by key. Put a cache in front of it, because reads outnumber writes a hundred to one. And keep the app servers stateless, behind a load balancer, so scaling out is just adding one.

q3-path.text: Follow one redirect through it. On a cache hit, that's two round trips inside the data center, about a millisecond by the ladder. A miss adds a third, to the store, and an SSD read: about one point six milliseconds.

q3-counter.text: The follow-up is the counter. One counter that every server asks is a bottleneck, and one more thing that can fail.

q3-guess.text: And counted IDs make consecutive keys, so anyone can walk through everyone's links. If that matters, scramble the ID before encoding it, or use the hash.

q4.text: Question four. What is a single point of failure, and how do you remove one? It's any component whose failure takes the system down. This diagram has three: one load balancer, one store, and one cache. Lose the cache, and every read lands on the store at once.

q4-fix.text: Remove each with redundancy. Run the load balancers as an active-passive pair, so a standby takes over when the active one dies. Replicate the store, with failover to a replica, and give the cache replicas too. Then spread it all across availability zones: separate data centers in one region.

q4-goal.text: The goal: no single machine's death causes an outage.

q4-retry.text: That's half the job. The other half is not burying a dependency that's already failing. Retries add load at the worst moment: in the page's simulation, they push it to three hundred requests a second, against a service that was failing at a hundred.

q4-states.text: A circuit breaker stops that. When errors pass half, it opens, and sends nothing for twelve seconds. Then it lets a tenth of the traffic through as a probe. Here the first probe still fails, so it opens again; the second passes, and it closes.

q4-close.text: Left alone, the service recovers. Under retries, it never does.

q5.text: Question five. What is a CDN, and when do you use one? It's a content delivery network: edge servers close to your users, caching what your origin serves.

q5-light.text: Distance sets a floor. Light in fiber covers about two hundred kilometers a millisecond, so a user in Sydney is at least a hundred and fifty-seven milliseconds, round trip, from a server in Virginia: over a hundred times the millisecond the redirect spends inside the data center. An edge server across town is under a millisecond away.

q5-use.text: So it cuts latency, takes traffic off your origin, and absorbs spikes. Use it for anything static or cacheable: images, JavaScript, CSS and video.

q5-redirect.text: A popular short link is the same redirect for everyone, so the edge can answer it too. The price: a click the edge answers never reaches your servers, so they can't count it, and a link you take down keeps working there until its time to live runs out. So keep that time short.

q5-win.text: For a read-heavy product with users everywhere, a CDN is the cheapest large win there is.

next.text: That's a first design. It's sized for its estimate, and no single machine can take it down.

next-10x.text: Now give it ten times the traffic. Next: scaling a design.

q3-blocks.text: Hand each server a block of IDs instead, say a million at a time, and it counts on its own.

q2-cache.text: Even a whole day of new links is five gigabytes, so the hot set fits in one machine's memory.

q3-temp.text: Make that redirect temporary. Browsers keep a permanent one, so later clicks never reach you: you can't count them, or take the link down.

q3-coord.text: The counter still hands out the blocks, but it's asked once per million IDs, and a server that dies just leaves a gap.

q3-edges.text: Custom aliases share the key space, stored only if free, and expiry is a column the redirect checks.

q4-how.text: So retry with backoff and jitter, under a small budget, and while the breaker is open, fail fast or serve a cached answer.

q5-dyn.text: Dynamic, user-specific responses usually bypass it, or get a short time to live: how long the edge may keep a copy. Even those save handshake round trips, since the connection ends at the edge.
